name: Mwimbi-Muthambi
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.verdict: a source was named but could not be reached
earlier_scan.source_named: Möhlig, Wilhelm J. G. 1974. Die Stellung der Bergdialekte im Osten des Mt. Kenya (dialect phonology covering Mwimbi-Muthambi; cited on Glottolog mwim1241; not online)

sources.citation: Erastus, Kanana Fridah. 2014. Noun morphophonemics and noun class restructuring: the case of Meru gender 11/10 restructuring. South African Journal of African Languages 34(1): 107-117.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Class 11/10 plural formation in six Meru dialects incl. Mwimbi and Muthambi; segmental only, no stress or tone.

sources.citation: Philippson, Gerard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique Orientale. These de Doctorat d'Etat, Universite Paris V, 542 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Group XXII (Thagicu) annex covers only Kamba and Kikuyu (pp. 513-514); Mwimbi appears once (p. 454, a 'porcupine' form cited from Bennett n.d.). Lists Moehlig 1974 as the only Embu/Meru prosodic source (p. 527). No Mwimbi/Meru stress statement.

sources.citation: Ford, K. C. 1976. Tone in Kikamba and the Central Kenya Bantu languages. Studies in African Linguistics 7(3): 261-293.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Tone study with Mwimbi (informant Erastus Rweria) and Muthambi (Kiraithe) data: two tone levels expandable to four (extra-high/extra-low), tone lexically distinctive in all eleven dialects, Mwimbi tone-form classes (13) and Muthambi (14) pp. 268-269, Mwimbi verb-form environments Appendix 1 p. 290. The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur anywhere in the article.

sources.citation: Kinegeni, Loyford Kariuki. 2024. A pragmatic analysis of Kimwimbi (E531) condolence messages. PhD thesis, Chuka University, 207 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Pragmatics; language background names Kimwimbi as E531 in the Meru cluster (Maho 2009). Nothing on stress or tone.

sources.citation: Kaburo, Diana Kananu. 2022. A syntactic analysis of raising structures in Kimuthambi. Journal of Linguistics, Literary, and Communication Studies (Chuka University) 1(2): 44-53.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Syntax only; identifies Kimuthambi as E531 Mwimbi-Muthambi. Nothing on stress or tone.

sources.citation: Kinyua, Ann Hidah & Peter Muriungi. 2016. Accounting for post-verbal affixes on the Kimwimbi verb. Research on Humanities and Social Sciences 6(20).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Verb-suffix morphology; one remark that passive/causative allomorphy 'is as a result of tone issues in actual utterance' (citing Marlo 2013). No stress statement.

sources.citation: Kanana, Fridah Erastus. 2011. Meru dialects: The linguistic evidence. Nordic Journal of African Studies 20(4): 300-327.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Consonant and vowel isoglosses across Imenti, Igoji, Upper/Lower Mwimbi, Upper/Lower Muthambi, Chuka, Tharaka (Dahl's law, fricative deletion, compensatory lengthening). Nothing on tone or stress.

sources.citation: Gacunku, Lucyline. 2005. A phonological investigation of irregularity and variation in the Kimeru nominal concordial system. MA thesis, University of Nairobi, 253 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Data are the author's native Mwimbi variety (p. 6 'We will focus on the Mwimbi variety, which is my native tongue'; fieldwork in Muthambi and Mwimbi divisions, p. 20). Segmental phonology and noun-class morphophonology only; p. 33: 'Aspects of tone however are outside our scope in this study.' No mention of stress.

sources.citation: Kaburo, Diana Kananu. 2024. A cartographic analysis of Kimuthambi clause structure. PhD thesis, Chuka University (full text).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, full text not open (only the abstract or a snippet is); only the abstract or a snippet was reachable when a reader tried
sources.note: Only the 7-page abstract is in the Chuka repository; a full PhD on Kimuthambi would have a language-background chapter that might state the tonal/stress facts, though it is a syntax thesis (low expectation).

sources.citation: Erastus, Kanana Fridah. 2015. Lexico-Phonological Comparative Analysis of Selected Dialects of the Meru-Tharaka Group. Schriften zur Afrikanistik 23. Frankfurt am Main: Peter Lang, 350 pp.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, paywalled at the publisher (DOI); library e-access not checked
sources.note: Modern comparative phonology of Imenti, Igoji, Tharaka, Mwimbi, Muthambi and Chuka based on fieldwork; the dialect-description chapters (4-6) may carry a suprasegmental note. Only the abstract is open (KU repository); the book is paywalled.

sources.citation: Ford, K. C. 1975. Tone and intonation in Kikamba. Research report, University of Nairobi, 164 pp. (ms.); and Clements, G. N. & K. C. Ford. In preparation. Tone in Kikuyu dialects.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Ford's fuller manuscript underlying the 1976 SAL article; the 1976 paper refers to it for the Muthambi 'flattening' examples (Ford 1975b) and the comparative dialect material. Unpublished; only a library copy at Nairobi could show whether stress is addressed.

sources.citation: Moehlig, Wilhelm J. G. 1974. Die Stellung der Bergdialekte im Osten des Mt. Kenya und ihr Verhaeltnis zum Kikuyu. Berlin: Dietrich Reimer, 249 pp. + 41 maps.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Comparative dialect phonology of the Mt. Kenya east-slope dialects (Mwimbi, Muthambi, Chuka, Tharaka, Imenti, Embu..); Philippson 1991 lists it as the only prosodic source for Embu/Meru, so it is the likeliest place for a statement on accent/tone in Mwimbi-Muthambi. Print only; the scan's own 'source named' item.

sources.citation: Bennett, Patrick R. 1969. A comparative study of four Thagicu verbal systems: the inflectional systems of Kikuyu, Kamba, Embu, and Mwimbi. PhD thesis, SOAS, University of London, 328 pp.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL8025.B4); ask your own library for a scan or interlibrary loan
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL8025 .B4
sources.note: The only full-length primary description with Mwimbi as one of four target languages (Glottolog's sole descriptive reference for mwim1241); a verbal-system thesis from SOAS in 1969 would normally carry a phonological introduction including tone and possibly stress. Not online: UoN record is metadata-only, SOAS eprints unreachable.

sources.citation: Bennett, Patrick R. 1981. Proto-Thagicu lexical reconstructions (ms./book, per Glottolog); and Bennett 1967 'Dahl's law in Thagicu' African Language Studies 8: 127-159; 1968 'An eight-vowel in Thagicu' Journal of African Languages 7: 140-155.

sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Comparative/historical Thagicu work drawing on Bennett's Mwimbi data; segmental in focus but the reconstructions may carry tone/accent marking conventions for Mwimbi. Gacunku 2005 cites 'Bennett (1981: 295)' on Mwimbi.
